title: Book 3
paragraphs: I came to Carthage, where a cauldron of illicit loves sang all around me. I wasn't in love yet, but I loved the idea of being in love, and beneath that lay a deeper want that made me hate myself for not wanting enough. I searched for something to love, in love with the very act of loving, and I hated safety and any path free of traps. Inside me was a famine for that inward food which is you, my God — yet the famine itself didn't make me hungry for you. I felt no longing at all for that incorruptible nourishment, not because I was full of it, but because the emptier I was, the more I recoiled from it. For this reason my soul was sick and covered in sores, and it flung itself outward, wretchedly, craving to be scraped raw by the touch of the senses. And yet, if the things I loved had had no soul in them, I could not have loved them. To love and to be loved was sweet to me — sweeter still when I actually got to enjoy the person I loved. So I fouled the spring of friendship with the filth of lust, and clouded its brightness with the darkness of desire; and foul and degraded as I was, out of sheer vanity I still wanted to pass for refined and sophisticated. I threw myself headlong into the very love I longed to be trapped by. My God, my mercy, with how much bitterness did you, in your great goodness, season that sweetness for me! I was loved in return, and secretly reached the point of enjoying my lover — and joyfully let myself be shackled with chains that would bring me sorrow, so that I could be whipped with the burning iron rods of jealousy, suspicion, fear, anger, and quarrels.

Stage plays carried me away too, full of images of my own miseries and fuel for my fire. Why is it that people want to feel sad watching sorrowful, tragic things onstage, when they would never willingly suffer the same things themselves? Yet as spectators they want to feel the grief, and that very grief is their pleasure. What is this but a wretched kind of madness? Because the less free a person is from these feelings, the more such scenes move him. When someone suffers his own misfortune, we call it misery; when he feels for someone else's, we call it compassion. But what kind of compassion is this, for made-up, staged suffering? The audience isn't being called on to help anyone — only to feel sad, and the more sadness the play draws out of him, the more he applauds the actor who produced it. And if the misfortunes of the characters — whether historical or purely invented — are performed in a way that doesn't move the audience to tears, he leaves annoyed and full of criticism; but if he's moved, he sits there absorbed, and weeps for the pleasure of it.

So is grief itself something we love? Surely everyone wants joy. Or is it that, while no one wants to be miserable himself, he's still glad to feel mercy for others — and since mercy can't exist without some pain, is that pain loved for that reason alone? This too flows from that same stream of friendship. But where does that stream go? Where does it flow to? Why does it rush into that boiling torrent of pitch, those monstrous swelling tides of foul lust, into which it willingly twists and transforms itself, hurling itself down and corrupting itself out of its own heavenly clarity? Should compassion, then, be thrown out? Certainly not. Let grief, then, sometimes be loved — but guard against uncleanness, my soul, under the protection of my God, the God of our fathers, who is to be praised and exalted above all things forever; guard against uncleanness. I haven't stopped feeling pity now; but back then, in the theaters, I rejoiced along with lovers when they sinfully enjoyed each other, even though it was only make-believe in the play. And when they lost each other, as though truly compassionate, I grieved with them — and yet took delight in both. But now I feel far more pity for someone who delights in his own wrongdoing than for someone thought to suffer by missing out on some destructive pleasure or losing some miserable so-called happiness. That is surely the truer mercy — but grief takes no pleasure in it. Because even though someone who grieves for the miserable is praised for his charity, someone with genuine compassion would rather there were nothing at all to grieve over. If ill will toward the good were even possible (which it never could be), then someone who truly and sincerely feels for others might wish there were miserable people to feel for. So some sorrow may be permitted — none should be loved. This is how you, Lord God, act: you love souls far more purely than we do, and your pity for them is untouched by any pain, though never less than perfect. And who is equal to this?

But I, wretched as I was, loved to grieve back then, and went looking for things to grieve over — so that when I watched someone else's misery, staged and pretended, the performance that pleased me most, and moved me most powerfully, was the one that drew tears out of me. Is it any wonder that I, an unhappy sheep straying from your flock and impatient with your care, caught a foul disease? Hence my love of griefs — not the kind that would cut deep into me, since I had no wish to suffer what I loved to watch, but the kind that, on hearing these invented stories, would lightly scratch the surface — and from that scratching, as from poisoned fingernails, came inflamed swelling, festering sores, and rot. Was a life like that, my God, really a life at all?

And your faithful mercy hovered over me from a distance. How many grave sins did I wear myself out committing, chasing a sacrilegious curiosity that, having abandoned you, was meant to lead me down into treacherous depths and the deceptive service of demons — to whom I offered up my wicked deeds as sacrifices, and in all of this you scourged me! I even dared, while your sacred rites were being celebrated inside the walls of your Church, to want and to pursue a scheme whose fruits deserved death — for which you punished me severely, though nowhere near as severely as my fault deserved, O you, my overflowing mercy, my God, my refuge from the terrible destroyers among whom I wandered, stiff-necked, drawing further away from you, loving my own ways instead of yours, loving a fugitive kind of freedom.

The studies then considered respectable were aimed at succeeding in the law courts — the more deceitful you were, the more praise you earned. Such is human blindness, that people even boast of their blindness. By now I was the top student in the school of rhetoric, and I gloried in it with pride, swelling up with arrogance — though, Lord, you know I was far quieter than, and entirely removed from, the destructive behavior of the so-called "Wreckers" (that ominous, devilish name was the very badge of their swagger), among whom I lived with a shameless kind of shame that I wasn't like them. I lived among them, and sometimes even enjoyed their friendship, even though I always despised what they actually did — that is, their "wrecking," by which they wantonly tormented the modesty of newcomers, disrupting it with cruel, gratuitous mockery, feeding their own malicious appetite on it. Nothing more closely resembles the actual behavior of demons than this. So what could they truly be called but "Wreckers" — themselves wrecked and thoroughly twisted first, secretly mocked and led astray by deceiving spirits, the very spirits that delight in mocking and deceiving others through them?

Among people like these, at that unsettled age of mine, I studied the books of eloquence, in which I longed to excel — for a damnable, vainglorious purpose, a delight in merely human vanity. In the ordinary course of my studies I came across a particular book by Cicero, whose style nearly everyone admires, if not his heart. This book of his contains an exhortation to philosophy, and it's called the Hortensius. That book changed the direction of my feelings, turned my prayers toward you, Lord, and gave me new purposes and desires. Every empty hope suddenly lost its value to me, and I longed, with an almost unbelievable burning desire, for the immortality that wisdom promises, and I began to rise up so that I might return to you. It wasn't to sharpen my tongue — which is what I seemed to be buying with my mother's money that year, my nineteenth, my father having died two years before — it wasn't to sharpen my tongue that I used that book; what shaped me wasn't its style but its substance.

How I burned then, my God, how I burned to rise up from earthly things back to you, though I had no idea what you meant to do with me! For wisdom is with you. But the love of wisdom is called, in Greek, "philosophy," and it was with this that the book set me on fire. There are those who lead people astray through philosophy, dressing up and disguising their own errors under that great, smooth, respectable name — and nearly everyone of that kind, in that age and in earlier ones, is criticized and exposed in that very book. There too is made plain that healthy warning given by your Spirit, through your good and devoted servant: "Beware that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deceit, following human tradition, following the basic principles of this world, and not following Christ; for in him the whole fullness of God dwells bodily." And since at that time — you, light of my heart, know this — I didn't yet know the writings of the apostles, I was delighted by that exhortation, but only to this extent: it strongly stirred me, kindled me, set me on fire to love, seek, obtain, hold on to, and embrace not this or that particular school of thought, but wisdom itself, whatever it turned out to be. The only thing that held me back, unlit as I still was, was that the name of Christ wasn't in it. That name — the name of my Savior, your Son — my tender heart had, by your mercy, Lord, devoutly drunk in with my mother's milk and kept stored deep within; and whatever lacked that name, however learned, polished, or true it was, couldn't fully take hold of me.

So I resolved to turn my mind to the holy Scriptures, to see what kind of thing they were. But what I found was a text not understood by the proud, not laid open to children — humble to approach, yet lofty in its depths, and wrapped in mysteries. And I wasn't the kind of person who could enter into it, or bow my neck to follow where it led. I didn't feel about those Scriptures then the way I speak of them now; to me they seemed unworthy of comparison with the grandeur of Cicero — my swollen pride recoiled from their plainness, and my sharp wit couldn't pierce down into their depths. Yet they were exactly the kind of writing that would grow along with a small child. But I refused to be small; puffed up with pride, I took myself for someone great.

So I fell in with men who were proudly deluded, thoroughly carnal, and endless talkers, in whose mouths were the devil's snares, baited with the syllables of your name, and the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, our Comforter. These names never left their mouths, but only as sound and noise on the tongue — their hearts were empty of truth. Still they shouted "Truth, Truth," and said a great deal about it to me, yet there was none of it in them. What they spoke was false — false not only about you, who alone truly are Truth, but even about the basic elements of this world, which are your creation. And really I ought to have passed over even the philosophers who spoke truthfully about such things, for love of you, my Father, supremely good, Beauty of all beautiful things. O Truth, Truth — how deeply, even then, did the very marrow of my soul long for you, when these men echoed your name to me again and again, in book after huge book, in every different way, though it was only an echo! And these were the dishes on which they served me — starving as I was for you — not you, but the sun and moon, beautiful works of yours, yes, but still only your works, not you yourself, and not even your first works. Because your spiritual creations come before these physical ones, however heavenly and bright they are. But I hungered and thirsted not even for those first works of yours, but for you yourself, the Truth, in whom there is no change, no shadow cast by shifting. And still they kept setting before me, on those dishes, glittering illusions — and it would have been better to love the actual sun, at least real to our sight, than those illusions that deceive the mind through the eyes. And yet, because I took them to be you, I fed on them — without much appetite, though, because you didn't taste to me, in them, the way you really are; you weren't those empty things, and I wasn't nourished by them, only worn down further. Food eaten in a dream looks very much like the food we eat awake, and yet the sleeper gains no nourishment from it, because he's asleep. But those things weren't even like you at all, in the way you've since spoken to me — they were mere physical fantasies, false bodies, and even the real bodies we see with our physical eyes, whether in the sky or on earth, are far more solid and certain than those fantasies; even animals and birds perceive real bodies just as we do, and they're more certain than anything we merely imagine. And we imagine real bodies with more certainty, in turn, than we can guess at other, vaster, infinite bodies that don't actually exist at all. That was the kind of empty husk I was feeding on then — and not being fed. But you, love of my soul, whom I search for so that I might grow strong, are not those bodies we see, even in the sky, nor those we don't see there either — because you created them, and you don't even count them among the greatest of your works. How far, then, are you from those fantasies of mine — fantasies of bodies that don't exist at all — compared to which even the mental images of real bodies are far more certain, and the real bodies themselves more certain still, though you are not even those; no, nor even the soul, which is what gives bodies life. So the life of bodies is better and more certain than the bodies themselves. But you are the life of souls, the life of every life, having life in yourself, and you never change — life of my soul.

Where were you to me then, and how far away? I had truly wandered far from you, shut out even from the very husks the pigs ate, on which I fed myself with husks. Because how much better are the fables of poets and grammarians than these traps? Verses, poems, and "Medea in flight" are truly more useful than these men's five elements, disguised in various forms, corresponding to five dens of darkness that don't exist at all, yet kill anyone who believes in them. I could turn verses and poems into real nourishment, and though I might sing of "Medea in flight," I never claimed it was true; though I heard it sung, I never believed it — but those other things, I did believe. How miserable, how miserable — by what steps was I dragged down into the depths of hell! Toiling and thrashing about for lack of truth, because I was seeking you, my God (I confess this to you now, who had mercy on me even before I confessed it), not through the understanding of the mind, by which you meant me to rise above the animals, but through the perception of the flesh. But you were more inward to me than my innermost self, and higher than my highest point. I ran into that bold woman pictured in Solomon — simple, and knowing nothing — sitting at the door and saying, "Eat bread taken in secret, gladly, and drink stolen water, for it is sweet." She seduced me, because she found my soul living out in the open, in the eye of my flesh, chewing over the very food it had devoured through that eye.

Beyond this, I didn't know what truly exists. And I was talked into agreeing, as though by sheer cleverness, with foolish deceivers when they asked me, "Where does evil come from?" "Is God confined to a bodily shape, with hair and fingernails?" "Should men who had many wives at once, who killed people, and sacrificed living creatures, be counted righteous?" These questions troubled me badly in my ignorance, and even as I drifted from the truth, I thought I was heading toward it — because I didn't yet know that evil is nothing but the absence of good, right down to the point where a thing stops existing altogether. And how could I have seen that, when my eyes could reach only as far as physical bodies, and my mind only as far as imagined images? I didn't know that God is a Spirit, not a being with parts stretched out in length and breadth, not a being whose existence is bulk — since any bulk is smaller in a part than in the whole, and if it's infinite, it must still be smaller in any part marked off by a given space than in its infinity, and so can't be wholly present everywhere the way spirit, the way God, is. And what it was in us that made us like God, so that we could rightly be called made in God's image, I had no idea at all.

Nor did I know true inward righteousness, which doesn't judge by custom but by the most rightful law of God Almighty — the law by which the customs of different places and times were arranged to fit those times and places, while the law itself remains everywhere and always the same, not one thing here and another there. By this law Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, and David were righteous, and all those God himself commends — yet foolish people judge them unrighteous, judging by their own human standards and measuring the moral customs of the entire human race against their own narrow habits. It's as if, in an armory, someone who doesn't know what belongs where should try to cover his head with shin guards or put his feet into a helmet, and then complain that they don't fit; or as if, on a day when business closes in the afternoon, someone got angry at not being allowed to keep his shop open, because he'd been allowed to that morning; or as if someone in one house noticed a servant handling something the butler isn't allowed to touch, or something permitted outdoors but forbidden in the dining room, and got angry that the same rule doesn't apply everywhere in one house and one household. That's exactly the position of people who are irritated to hear that something was once lawful for righteous men that isn't now, or that God commanded one thing to them and another to later people, even though both were obeying the same righteousness — when they can plainly see, in a single person, on a single day, in a single household, that different things suit different parts, and that something once allowed becomes not allowed after a certain time, permitted or commanded in one place but rightly forbidden and punished in another. Is justice, then, variable or changeable? No — but the times it presides over don't all flow the same way, because they are, after all, times. But people, whose own days on earth are few, can't reconcile — through their limited senses — the causes at work in earlier ages and other nations, which they never experienced, with the causes at work in their own times, which they have; whereas in one body, one day, one household, they can easily see what suits each limb, season, part, and person. To the one they raise objections; to the other they simply submit.

I didn't know or notice these things back then; they were right in front of my eyes on every side, and I didn't see them. I wrote poems, and in them I couldn't put any given syllable anywhere I liked — different meters required different arrangements, and even within a single meter the same syllable couldn't go just anywhere. Yet the art by which I wrote didn't have separate rules for each of these different cases — it held them all within one single art. Still, I couldn't see how the righteousness that good and holy people obeyed held together, far more excellently and sublimely, in a single whole, all the things God commanded, without varying in any part — even though, across different times, it didn't prescribe everything all at once, but assigned and required what was fitting for each. And in my blindness I condemned the holy fathers of old, not only for making use of what was appropriate to their own time, as God commanded and inspired them, but even for foretelling things to come, exactly as God was revealing those things through them.

Can it ever, at any time or place, be wrong to love God with your whole heart, your whole soul, and your whole mind, and to love your neighbor as yourself? So those foul offenses against nature — like those of the men of Sodom — are always and everywhere to be despised and punished. Even if every nation on earth committed them, they would all stand equally guilty under God's law, which never made people to abuse one another that way. Because the very relationship that should exist between God and us is violated when the nature he authored is defiled by perverse lust. But offenses against human custom are to be avoided according to whatever custom prevails in each place, so that something agreed upon and settled by the custom or law of any city or nation may not be broken by the lawless whim of anyone, citizen or foreigner — because any part that doesn't fit with its whole is offensive. But when God commands something, against the customs or agreements of some people, even something never done by them before, it must be done — and if it's been let lapse, it must be restored; and if it was never established, it must now be established. Because if it's lawful for a king, in the state he governs, to command something no one before him, and not even he himself before now, had commanded, and obeying him can't be against the common good of the state — in fact it would be against the common good not to obey him, since obeying rulers is a general compact of human society — how much more unhesitatingly ought we to obey God in everything he commands, he who rules over all his creation! Just as, among human authorities, the greater power is obeyed ahead of the lesser, so God must be obeyed above all.

So too with acts of violence, where there's a wish to hurt someone, whether by insult or injury — whether for revenge, as one enemy strikes another, or for some gain at another's expense, as a robber preys on a traveler, or to avoid some harm, as against someone feared, or out of envy, as when someone less fortunate resents someone more so, or someone who's done well resents someone whose equal standing to himself he fears or resents — or purely for the pleasure of another's pain, like spectators at gladiator fights, or people who jeer and mock others. These are the roots of wrongdoing that spring from the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, or the lust for power — alone, in pairs, or all three together — and so people live badly against the three and the seven, that ten-stringed harp, your Ten Commandments, God most high and most sweet. But what foul offenses can there really be against you, who can't be defiled? Or what acts of violence against you, who can't be harmed? Yet you punish what people do against themselves, because even when they sin against you, they're acting wickedly against their own souls — and wrongdoing gives itself the lie, by corrupting and twisting the nature you created and ordained for them, whether through excessive use of things that are allowed, or by burning with desire, in things not allowed, for uses that go against nature; or they're found guilty, raging in heart and speech against you, kicking against the goads; or when, breaking through the boundaries of human society, they boldly delight in forming reckless alliances or divisions, depending on whatever they want to gain or whatever offends them. And all this happens whenever you are abandoned, Fountain of Life, the only true Creator and Ruler of the universe — when, out of self-willed pride, some single false thing is picked out from your creation and loved instead of you. So it's through humble devotion that we return to you; and you cleanse us of our bad habits, and show mercy to the sins of those who confess, and hear the groaning of the prisoner, and loosen the chains we made for ourselves — as long as we don't raise against you the horns of a false freedom, losing everything through greed for more, by loving our own private good more than you, the good of everyone.

Among these offenses of foulness and violence, and so many other wrongs, there are also the sins of people who are, on the whole, making progress — sins that those who judge rightly, by the standard of perfection, still find fault with, even while commending the people themselves, in hope of future fruit, the way you'd praise the green blade of growing corn. And there are some things that look like offenses of foulness or violence but aren't really sins, because they offend neither you, our Lord God, nor human society — for instance, when things suited to a given time are acquired for the needs of life, and we can't tell whether it's out of simple greed for possessions; or when things are punished by lawful authority for the sake of correction, and we can't tell whether it's out of a desire to hurt. Many an action disapproved of by people is approved by your judgment; and many an action praised by people is condemned, you being witness — because the outward appearance of the act, the mind of the one doing it, and the unknown demands of the moment can all vary separately. But when you suddenly command something unusual and unexpected — even something you'd once forbidden, and you still, for the time being, hide the reason for your command — and it goes against the established custom of some human society, who could doubt it should be done, since the society that serves you is the just one? But blessed are those who know your commands! Because everything your servants did was done either to show something needed for the present moment, or to foreshadow things still to come.

Not knowing any of this, I mocked your holy servants and prophets. And what did I gain by mocking them, except to be mocked by you in turn, as I was drawn along, little by little, without noticing, into believing such follies as that a fig tree wept when it was picked, and that the tree, its mother, shed tears of milk? And yet, if some "Elect" Manichaean saint had eaten that very fig — picked, mind you, through someone else's sin, not his own — and mixed it into his own body, he would supposedly breathe out angels from it; particles of divinity would burst forth from him at every groan or sigh of his prayers — particles of the most high and true God that had stayed trapped inside that fig unless freed by the teeth or stomach of some "Elect" saint! And I, wretched fool, believed that more mercy was owed to the fruits of the earth than to the human beings they were created for. Because if someone hungry — someone who wasn't a Manichaean — asked for a bite, giving it to him would seem, to us, practically a capital crime.

And you reached your hand down from above and pulled my soul up out of that deep darkness — through my mother, your faithful servant, weeping to you for me more than mothers weep over the physical deaths of their children. Because through the faith and the spirit she had received from you, she recognized the death I was living in, and you heard her, Lord; you heard her and didn't despise her tears, when they streamed down and watered the ground beneath her eyes wherever she prayed — yes, you heard her. How else explain the dream by which you comforted her, so that she agreed to let me live with her and eat at the same table in the house — something she'd begun to refuse, loathing and detesting the blasphemies of my false belief? In the dream she saw herself standing on a kind of wooden rule or measuring rod, and a radiant young man came toward her, cheerful, smiling at her, while she stood grieving, overwhelmed with sorrow. He asked her — the way such figures do, to instruct rather than to be instructed — what was causing her grief and her daily tears, and when she answered that she was mourning my ruin, he told her to be at peace, and to look and see that "where she was, there I was too." And when she looked, she saw me standing beside her on that same rule. What could this be, except that your ears were turned toward her heart? O good and all-powerful one, who cares for each of us as if you cared for him alone, and for all of us as if we were only one!

How else explain what happened next, when she told me this vision, and I tried to twist it to mean that she, rather, shouldn't give up hope of one day being what I was — she answered at once, without any hesitation at all: "No — because I wasn't told, 'where he is, you will be too,' but 'where you are, he will be too.'" I confess to you, Lord, that as far as I can remember (and I've often spoken of this), your answer, delivered through my wide-awake mother — the fact that she wasn't thrown off by the plausible spin I put on it, and saw at once what needed to be seen, which I myself certainly hadn't grasped until she said it — moved me even more, at the time, than the dream itself, by which the joy of this holy woman, though it would only be fulfilled so long afterward, was foretold that far in advance, to comfort her present anguish. Because nearly nine years passed in which I wallowed in the mud of that deep pit and the darkness of falsehood, often trying to rise, but each time knocked down harder. Through all that time, that chaste, devout, and level-headed widow — exactly the kind you love — though now somewhat more hopeful, never let up on her weeping and mourning, and never stopped, at every hour of prayer, grieving over my case before you. And her prayers reached your presence — and yet you still allowed me to stay tangled, and tangled again, in that darkness.

Meanwhile you gave her another answer, which I recall — because I'm passing over a great deal, hurrying toward the things that press on me more urgently to confess to you, and much I simply don't remember. You gave her, then, another answer, through one of your priests — a certain bishop, raised in your Church and well versed in your books. When this woman asked him to be willing to talk with me, refute my errors, unteach me what was wrong, and teach me what was right (which he was in the habit of doing, when he found people ready to receive it), he refused — wisely, as I realized only later. He answered that I was still unteachable, puffed up with the novelty of that heresy, and that I'd already tripped up a number of unskilled people with clever, tricky questions, as she had told him. "But leave him alone for a while," he said, "just pray to God for him. He'll find out for himself, through his own reading, what that error is and how deep its wrongness goes." At the same time he told her how he himself, as a boy, had been handed over to the Manichees — a heretical sect claiming secret spiritual knowledge, which Augustine belonged to for years — by his own misguided mother, and had not only read almost all their books but had copied out most of them by hand — and had seen, without needing anyone to argue him out of it or prove anything to him, just how much that sect deserved to be avoided, and had avoided it. When he'd said this and she still wasn't satisfied, but kept pressing him, pleading and in tears, to see me and talk with me, he — a little irritated now by her persistence — said, "Go your way; God bless you. It isn't possible that the son of these tears should be lost." She often mentioned afterward, in conversations with me, that she took that answer as though it had come down from heaven itself.
